wt - LLM Quick Context

Audience
- This file is for LLMs and coding agents that index or enter this repository.
- It serves two audiences: (1) users of the wt tool, and (2) contributors changing wt source code.

What wt is
- wt is a Git worktree manager written in Go.
- It creates, checks out, lists, and removes worktrees with predictable paths.

Section A: Using wt (installed tool consumers)
- Use this section if you are helping someone USE wt, not modify this repository.
- Primary commands:
  - wt clone <owner/repo|url> [dest] (alias: wt cl) — acquire the main repo under repo_root
  - wt create <branch> [base-branch]
  - wt checkout <branch> (alias: wt co)
  - wt cd <branch> (alias: wt sw) — switch to an existing worktree; never creates one
  - wt list (alias: wt ls)
  - wt remove <branch> (alias: wt rm)
  - wt pr [number|url] (requires gh)
  - wt mr [number|url] (requires glab)
  - wt copy [branch] [--dry-run] [--force] [--from <branch|path>] — materialise [files] into a worktree
  - wt info
  - wt init
- Typical consumer workflow:
  1) wt create feat/short-description
  2) Work in the created worktree
  3) wt ls to inspect worktrees
  4) wt rm <branch> when done
- Consumer checks:
  - No Go test/build/e2e steps are required to use an installed wt binary.

Section B: Contributing to wt (project authors/maintainers)
- Use this section only when modifying files in this repository.
- Contributor workflow rule:
  - Do not switch branches in the main checkout for task work.
  - Create an isolated worktree per task with wt create.
- Contributor validation checks:
  - go test ./...
  - go build -o bin/wt .
  - go run e2e/run.go

Configuration and hooks
- Config file: ~/.config/wt/config.toml (or WT_CONFIG / --config)
- Per-repo override: .wt.toml in the repo root (project policy; ignores root, repo_root, repo_pattern, clone hooks)
- Git config: wt.root, wt.repoRoot, wt.strategy, wt.pattern, wt.separator, wt.repoPattern, wt.copyIgnored, wt.copy, wt.link, wt.exclude via git config --local/--global
- wt.copy/wt.link/wt.exclude are multi-valued: 'git config --add' for each pattern, --unset-all to clear; the other keys are scalars
- Never read from git config at any scope: [hooks], hooks_policy and [trust] — git config is settings, never commands nor the policy gating them
- Git config key spelling: the TOML key with sections flattened and multi-word names camelCased; git rejects "_" in a key name, and one such line makes the whole config file unparseable
- Key settings: root, strategy, pattern, separator, repo_root, repo_pattern
- Env overrides: WORKTREE_ROOT, WORKTREE_STRATEGY, WORKTREE_PATTERN, WORKTREE_SEPARATOR, WT_REPO_ROOT, WT_REPO_PATTERN, WT_COPY_IGNORED
- Precedence (highest first): env > local git config > .wt.toml > config file > global git config > defaults
  (--config / WT_CONFIG select which TOML file is loaded; they are not a precedence level)
- Clone placement (wt clone): repo_root (default ~/dev/repos) + repo_pattern (default {.repoRoot}/{.repo.Host}/{.repo.Owner}/{.repo.Name}/{.branch})
- There is no built-in category concept: add a grouping segment yourself via {.env.VARNAME} in repo_pattern
- Environment variable defaults: {.env.VARNAME:-fallback} uses "fallback" when VARNAME is unset; {.env.VARNAME} without :- still errors on missing (catches typos)
- Supported hooks: pre/post create, checkout, remove, pr, mr, clone
- Hook env vars: WT_PATH, WT_BRANCH, WT_MAIN, WT_REPO_NAME, WT_REPO_HOST, WT_REPO_OWNER
- Under cmd /c only, hooks are skipped when a hook env value contains & | < > ^ " or a line break: cmd expands %WT_PATH% while parsing, so it would run as syntax, and the pattern/branch that put it there is not a hook command an approval covers. sh -c substitutes after parsing and is unaffected
- Disable hooks: WT_HOOKS_DISABLED=1
- NO hook runs until approved, wherever it came from — a repo's committed .wt.toml AND your own config file (since wt 0.4.0). Exactly two things stand in for that approval, both of them yours to set and neither reachable from a repo: a matching [trust] rule (config file only) and WT_HOOKS_APPROVE_ALL=1. trusted-only is not one — it runs approved hooks without prompting and skips the rest
- Approve: 'wt trust' (approves every source that applies here), 'wt trust --list', 'wt untrust' (this repo), 'wt untrust --global' (your config file)
- An approval is pinned to (scope, sha256 of that source's hook commands); scope is the repository for a .wt.toml, "user config" for your config file
- A path git prints is read with only its line ending trimmed, never TrimSpace: on Unix a directory whose name ends in a space is a different directory, and a `pattern` ending in a literal space would otherwise pin its approval to the scope of the space-less sibling
- Editing a hook command re-prompts; editing anything else in the file does not. An identical .wt.toml in another repository is not covered
- Approvals live in ~/.config/wt/trust.toml (version 2); pre-0.4 records pinned file bytes, are not translated, and are dropped with a warning
- The store path is always absolute: a non-absolute XDG_CONFIG_HOME (or APPDATA on Windows) is ignored with a warning per the XDG spec, so trust.toml never resolves against the working tree wt happens to be run from. An absolute one names the same directory in every repo, so pointing it into a working tree is a choice about where your approvals live, not something a repo can cause
- If no absolute config dir can be found at all — none of XDG_CONFIG_HOME, APPDATA, HOME — wt records nothing and treats every hook as unapproved; set one, or use WT_HOOKS_APPROVE_ALL=1 for automation you control
- [trust] whitelist (config file only): prefix = ["~/src/mine"], exact = ["~/src/acme/api"] — matching repos run hooks unasked and unrecorded; prefix matches whole path segments
- A [trust] rule is only matched against a repository identity git confirmed: wt looks for the current working tree in `git worktree list --porcelain -z` off the repo's common git dir. Unconfirmed, the approval is pinned to the directory's own path and no rule can cover it — a rule is a claim about repositories, and an unconfirmed key is just where a directory sits. -z because a worktree path may hold a newline, which the line-based format prints raw (git <2.36 gets the line read, and what it cannot confirm cannot match a rule)
- [trust] rules are literal paths: "~" expands, environment variables do not, and a rule containing "$" or "%" is ignored and reported ("$SRC/Users" would collapse to "/Users"). Both a rule and the path it is compared against are resolved the same way, with the symlinks above them followed even where the directory does not exist yet: a rule is written before the tree is filled at least as often as after, and a migrate destination is never there at all — a ~/src pointing at another volume otherwise leaves "~/src/mine" and "~/src/mine/tool" comparing equal to nothing, so a repo migrates into a whitelisted tree and runs its hooks unasked. A rule wt cannot follow to an end names no directory and is ignored with a warning; a destination it cannot follow skips the move. Rules that are relative, or name a filesystem root, are rejected too. Whitespace-only entries are skipped; a trailing space inside a rule is part of the directory name and is not trimmed (on Windows the OS strips it anyway, so such a rule reaches the space-less directory)
- hooks_policy (config file or WT_HOOKS_POLICY): prompt-untrusted (default), prompt-all, trusted-only, off
- prompt-all re-confirms even approved and whitelisted hooks; trusted-only never prompts and is the CI choice
- hooks_policy is never read from a repo-level .wt.toml; WT_HOOKS_APPROVE_ALL=1 skips the approval check (automation only), but does not override "off"/WT_HOOKS_DISABLED
- Absolute is not the test; "names one directory wherever wt runs" is (namesOneDirectory = IsAbs && !pathIsProcessRelative), applied to --config/WT_CONFIG, XDG_CONFIG_HOME/APPDATA (which is where the trust store lives), the HOME they fall back to, the ~ in a [trust] rule, and GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL. HOME matters most: asking it of the overrides only would refuse XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/proc/self/cwd/.config and then accept HOME=/proc/self/cwd behind it, and the trust store is a separate file from the config file wt also refuses — a repo committing .config/wt/trust.toml with its own scope and hash arrives pre-approved. A [trust] rule of "~/trees/*" under that home whitelists whatever is checked out in the working directory, reachable via --config/WT_CONFIG which name the file directly. A --config / WT_CONFIG / XDG_CONFIG_HOME under /proc/self, /proc/thread-self or /proc/<numeric pid> is refused: /proc/self/cwd is the working directory wearing an absolute spelling, and containment tests walk its lexical parents, which are /proc/self and /proc. Matched by name, not resolved — resolving would also catch the dotfiles symlink wt deliberately allows; what is wrong is that where the path leads depends on when you ask. A numeric pid is the same trick aimed at another process: the shell wt was launched from has its cwd inside the repository too
- A relative --config / WT_CONFIG is refused outright: it names a different file per directory, so the checkout supplies it (and "../wt-user.toml" reaches the superproject that vendored a submodule)
- An absolute one naming a file inside the repo you are in is refused too, with a warning: read as your config it could whitelist itself via [trust]. The name need not be .wt.toml. Containment is case folded and identity-checked — a differently-cased spelling of the repo's own directory opens the same committed file on macOS/Windows, and a macOS firmlink or Linux bind mount gives the repo a second absolute path; sameFile only knows about .wt.toml
- "Inside the repo" means any working tree of it, not the one you are standing in: the repo's own root, its common git dir and the directory holding it, and every path in `git worktree list -z`. A linked worktree is the same repository choosing the same committed bytes, and `--config ../main/.wt.toml` from one of them was the whole repo-config layer read as your config file
- Judged as written, not as resolved: a config symlinked from a dotfiles repo still applies while you stand in that repo (refusing it would move your worktrees). The one symlink refused targets the current repo's own .wt.toml, which would gain user-config scope
- A repo's .wt.toml may set pattern, and an absolute pattern is not anchored in root — but wt refuses one landing on its own config dir, a dir containing it, or your config file: the checked-out files would BECOME config.toml and trust.toml, supplying the gate rather than passing it. Compared with symlinks resolved as far as each path exists, case folded (~/.config/WT is the same directory on macOS/Windows), and by filesystem identity where both sides exist — EvalSymlinks does not touch a macOS firmlink, so /System/Volumes/Data{.env.HOME}/.config/wt was a one-line walk past a name comparison
- Two more folds in that comparison: a dangling symlink is followed to its target rather than treated as a missing directory (a ~/.config/wt into an uncloned dotfiles repo is the ordinary setup, and writing the target is what makes it live), and on Windows the not-yet-existing tail has trailing dots/spaces stripped as Win32 strips them, so "{.env.APPDATA}/wt." reaches %APPDATA%\wt while matching no name
- The same refusal covers git's own global config — ~/.gitconfig, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git (~/.config/git), and an absolute GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL. core.hooksPath is a hook command under another name: a branch checked out over ~/.config/git supplies git's config plus a hooks/ dir, and the next `git worktree add` runs it, in every repository afterwards and outside wt's gate entirely. Also the files that config pulls in: every include.path / includeIf.*.path read from `git config --global --show-origin`, with a relative value resolved the way git resolves it — against the directory of the declaring config file, so "dotfiles/gitconfig" in ~/.gitconfig is ~/dotfiles — and without evaluating the condition (whether it is included HERE is not the question — it is included wherever it matches, and the placement is what puts the file there). git ignores an include whose file is absent rather than complaining, so ~/dotfiles you have not cloned is an armed slot, not a broken setting
- git's global config covers ~/.gitconfig, $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/git AND the config file in it, GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM; includes are read from both --global and --system scopes
- A file a SUPERPROJECT committed cannot be the user config file either: a submodule is its own repository and the repo containing it is more committed content (repoWorkingTrees walks --show-superproject-working-tree)
- KNOWN GAP (issue #155): an approval is scoped to a path with no incarnation identifier, so deleting an approved checkout and re-cloning a different repo to the same path with PLAIN git (not `wt clone`, which prunes) inherits the approval if the hook command string matches
- The trust store FILE is guarded as well as the directory holding it: trust.toml is often a symlink out of a dotfiles repo, and a dangling one is a path a pattern can render onto
- git config includes are enumerated with --includes: `git config --global` turns include expansion OFF by default, so without it an [include] inside an included file is invisible
- Also refused: ANY path with a .git component, case-folded and asked both as written and once resolved (a symlink hides that a name is one), the repository's own common git dir, and the settings naming somewhere else git runs something from: core.hooksPath, init.templateDir, GIT_TEMPLATE_DIR, core.fsmonitor. A RELATIVE value is resolved against the working-tree top and guarded there, not dropped: core.hooksPath = ../shared-hooks leaves the repository. init.templateDir is the widest — git copies its hooks/ into every repository created afterwards. A ~user/... value is expanded the way git expands it. Not exhaustive over git's program-naming settings (core.pager, gpg.program name binaries you already have); the bounded fix is issue #154. Any repository's, not just the current one: ~/src/victim/.git/hooks is as reachable from a pattern as your own. Bare repos have no .git in the path (git init --bare /srv/git/project keeps hooks at /srv/git/project/hooks), so the name is not what is asked: every EXISTING directory above the destination goes to `git rev-parse --resolve-git-dir` and a placement inside one that answers is refused — git decides what a git directory is, not the spelling. Walk continues past a missing parent (a nonexistent dir answers "no"), bounded at 64 levels. A working TREE does not answer, so ordinary destinations are unaffected. `git worktree add` checks out into an existing EMPTY directory, and .git/hooks is empty on any clone made with no init template — a branch whose tree is one executable post-checkout, placed there, is run by the very next `git worktree add`, wt's own included. Shortest path from a committed pattern to arbitrary code, and it never reaches the gate
- A RELATIVE GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL or XDG_CONFIG_HOME is not guardable and wt says so on stderr (once per variable per process): git resolves either per working directory, so a repo committing a file by that name supplies the global config — read the moment any git command runs there, with no placement to refuse. XDG_CONFIG_HOME is the quieter of the two: wt ignores a non-absolute value for its own config dir while git honours it for git's. An EMPTY GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL is safe (git reads no global config at all). The guard stops there on purpose — it covers wt's config and the config of the program wt drives; an absolute pattern may still render elsewhere in $HOME (git worktree add will not write into a non-empty directory, so it reaches only paths nothing has created). To outrank a repo's pattern: `git config wt.pattern` in .git/config, or WORKTREE_PATTERN — not the config file, which .wt.toml overrides by design
- wt migrate skips the primary checkout when the origin URL does not resolve under ~/src: owner/name are parsed from the remote and filepath.Join cleans, so "x/../../.config" + "wt" reaches ~/.config/wt
- wt migrate also skips a primary whose destination is covered by a [trust] rule when its current path is not: the target is ~/src/{owner}/{name} off the origin URL and the host is dropped, so evil.example/acme lands in the ~/src/acme you whitelisted for github.com/acme. Moving it there by hand still works — then the path is your choice
- wt migrate also skips a primary whose destination answers to a command set its current path does not: records are keyed on (scope, sha256 of the commands) and outlive the checkout, so a repository named acme/tool shipping "make setup" inherits what the acme/tool you deleted left at ~/src/acme/tool. Compared as hash sets — "does the current path have an approval" would let an approval of this repo's older hooks launder a move onto a different set
- Both migrate checks fold the destination and not the source: it does not exist yet, so an origin URL ending "tool..git" renders a "tool." that matches no rule and no record and is then created by Win32 as the "tool" both name. Case folds too. The source is compared exactly, because crediting IT with an approval is what waives the refusal; granting is exact everywhere (~/src/Mine and ~/src/mine are two directories on Linux)
- wt migrate re-checks every destination against wtStateAtPath immediately before each move, not just when planning: the primary moves first and materialises its committed files, so a "link -> ../../../.config" in it is dangling at plan time and live by the time linked worktrees move through it
- wt clone derives placement from URL fields, so host/owner/name/branch may not contain a ".." segment, a "$" or "%", or a leading "~": the rendered path is expanded, and "$HOME/.config" is not a directory name. Every refusal points at the [dest] argument — an explicit destination is the user choosing the path. The final destination is checked against wt's own state on BOTH routes, including an explicit [dest]: a repo cloned into ~/.config/wt supplies config.toml and a committed trust.toml, so the escape hatch is another path, not permission to name that one
- wt clone discards trust records scoped to its destination before cloning, and reports the count (stale_approvals_dropped in JSON): the destination must be empty, and empty is what says the repository those records were given to is gone. Otherwise a namespace takeover, or a repo_pattern rendering onto an old checkout's path, arrives holding an approval you gave something else. migrate refuses instead of pruning because there the path comes from the origin URL, not from you
- Both of those match a record's scope at-or-under the path, not equal to it: a submodule's scope is <super>/.git/modules/<name>, which sits beneath the superproject's .git and answers for commands that run when the superproject is checked out. Equality prunes the parent and leaves the children behind
- Non-interactive runs (scripts, CI, --format json) decline and report on stderr rather than failing the command

Untracked file materialisation ([files])
- [files] schema: copy = [...], link = [...], exclude = [...] (gitignore syntax), copy_ignored = false
- Runs automatically on create/checkout/pr/mr, after 'git worktree add' and before post_* hooks; failure is non-fatal
- .worktreeinclude at the MAIN worktree root (gitignore syntax, one pattern per line) is unioned into copy; meant to be committed
- The three list keys are a UNION across layers, not a precedence contest: git config (global) -> config file -> repo .wt.toml -> git config (local) -> .worktreeinclude
- That order is display order only (duplicates dropped, credited to the leftmost layer); no layer overrides another, so which layer a pattern came from never changes the outcome
- exclude is applied last and cannot be overridden by any layer's copy or by copy_ignored; exclude and link reject negated (!) patterns
- To drop an inherited copy pattern, deny it from any layer: a "!" entry in copy beats every copy pattern and copy_ignored regardless of layer. link has no "!" form — only exclude stops an inherited link
- copy_ignored is a scalar and follows the normal precedence chain, spelled wt.copyIgnored in git config
- Candidates come from 'git ls-files --others --ignored --exclude-standard': tracked files are NEVER copied
- Never copied regardless of patterns: .git/ .bzr/ .hg/ .jj/ .pijul/ .sl/ .svn/ and any registered worktree of the same repo
- Copy method: reflink on APFS/Btrfs/XFS, buffered copy elsewhere (incl. Windows); symlinks recreated as symlinks, never dereferenced
- Existing destination files are skipped, not overwritten, unless --force; link entries are never replaced even with --force
- Disable: --no-copy on create/checkout/pr/mr, or WT_FILES_DISABLED=1
- [files] needs no 'wt trust' approval: it is declarative data held by invariants F1-F7 (see docs/configuration.md#files)
- JSON: 'wt copy --format json' emits {source, destination, dry_run, summary, files[{path, action, method, bytes, target, reason}]};
  create/checkout/pr/mr payloads gain a "files" summary object when anything was materialised

Dependencies
- Required: git
- Optional: gh (for wt pr), glab (for wt mr)
- Build from source: Go 1.24+

Canonical docs
- README.md: user-facing command usage, config, examples
- AGENTS.md: agent workflow and guardrails for repo changes
- CONTRIBUTING.md: contribution workflow and CI expectations

Non-interactive execution note
- For agent/CI contexts, prefer explicit args over interactive prompts:
  - wt co <branch>
  - wt cd <branch>
  - wt rm <branch>
  - wt pr <id>
  - wt mr <id>
